entry.name: Wheelbarrow
entry.desc: A wheelbarrow is a small hand-propelled vehicle, usually with one wheel, pushed and guided by a single person using two handles at the rear. The earliest evidence comes from Han dynasty China: a painted tomb mural at Chengdu in Sichuan, dated to 118 CE, shows a man pushing one. The Records of the Three Kingdoms credit the minister Zhuge Liang with a 'wooden ox' that carried military supplies in 231 CE. Chinese wheelbarrows mostly carried the load over a large central wheel, while those that appeared in medieval Europe between 1170 and 1250 had the wheel at or near the front.

row.label: Wheelbarrow
row.contested: The Records of the Three Kingdoms credit Zhuge Liang with its invention in 231 CE; M. J. T. Lewis read a 'one-wheeler' in temple inventories at Eleusis of 408–406 BCE as a Greek wheelbarrow, but there is no evidence for it in Greece or Rome.

notes: Zhuge Liang left out of people: the Chengdu mural is a century older than his wooden ox. European wheelbarrows not given as an independent origin: the article reports the consensus (Gille, Matthies, Needham) that it spread from China.

entry.name: Hot air balloon
entry.desc: A hot air balloon is a lighter-than-air aircraft whose envelope holds heated air, with a basket or gondola for passengers and a source of heat hung beneath it. The French brothers Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier developed one at Annonay in Ardèche and flew it unmanned in public in September 1783. On 21 November 1783 Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and François Laurent d'Arlandes made the first untethered manned flight, in Paris, in a Montgolfier balloon. The French used a balloon for observation at the battle of Fleurus in 1794, and Ed Yost and Jim Winker developed modern balloons with an onboard heat source from the 1950s.

row.label: Hot-air balloon
row.contested: Sky lanterns, used for military signals by Zhuge Liang in the Three Kingdoms era, were a precursor; in 1709 Bartolomeu de Gusmão showed an unmanned demonstration of his Passarola to John V of Portugal at the Casa da Índia.

notes: civ left empty: the brothers worked privately (the king only decreed who should fly first). Julian Nott's Nazca balloon hypothesis left out as speculation.

entry.name: Parachute
entry.desc: A parachute is a device that slows an object's descent through an atmosphere by creating drag. The oldest known design appears in a manuscript of the 1470s attributed to Francesco di Giorgio Martini, a man hanging from a conical canopy, and Leonardo da Vinci sketched a pyramidal one about 1485. Louis-Sébastien Lenormand made the first recorded public jump, in France in 1783, and coined the word in 1785. André Garnerin made the first descent under a frameless silk canopy in 1797, Gleb Kotelnikov invented the knapsack parachute in 1911, and in World War I observers escaped from tethered balloons by parachute.

row.label: Parachute
row.contested: In 852 Armen Firman jumped from a tower in Córdoba wearing a large cloak; Faust Vrančić's jump of 1617 from St Mark's Campanile in Venice probably never took place. The first recorded jump with a parachute was Lenormand's in 1783.

notes: Dated to the 1470s design, which the article calls the earliest evidence of an intentional parachute (Lynn White: the origin of 'the parachute as we know it'); the editor may prefer Lenormand's first jump, 1783, France, the article's 'modern parachute'. Place 'Italy' from the 'Italian' artist-engineers: the article does not say where the manuscript was made.

entry.name: Helicopter
entry.desc: A helicopter is a rotorcraft whose lift and thrust come from horizontally spinning rotors, so that it can take off and land vertically and hover. Chinese children played with bamboo flying toys from around 400 BCE, and Leonardo da Vinci designed an 'aerial screw' in the early 1480s. In 1907 the Breguet brothers' Gyroplane No. 1 lifted its pilot about 0.6 metres while men held it steady, and on 13 November 1907 Paul Cornu's machine made the first free flight with a pilot, in France. The Focke-Wulf Fw 61 of 1936 was the first practical helicopter, and Igor Sikorsky's R-4 of 1942 the first in full-scale production.

row.label: Helicopter
row.contested: Hermann Ganswindt's helicopter may have carried people in Berlin-Schöneberg in July 1901, but the film of the flight is lost; the Breguet machine was held steady by a man at each corner, so Cornu's flight of 13 November 1907 is reported as the first free one.

notes: The article calls the internal combustion engine the watershed that let helicopters lift people. Place only 'France': the article gives no town for either 1907 flight. The Gyroplane flight's date is uncertain (14 August to 29 September 1907), so the year rests on both flights.

entry.name: Junk
entry.desc: A junk is a Chinese sailing ship with a central rudder, an overhanging flat transom, watertight bulkheads and a flat bottom, built with iron nails and clamps. It grew from tapering rafts rather than dugout canoes, and Chinese junks were at first river craft with square sails. Under the Song dynasty (960–1279) they took up ocean-going features from Southeast Asian ships: Zhu Yu's Pingzhou Table Talks, published by 1119, describes hulls divided by bulkheads, and the battened junk sail was adopted around the 12th century. Under the Yuan, Chinese trade ships displaced Southeast Asian ones on their Indian Ocean routes.

row.label: Junk
row.contested: A pottery model of a ship with a stern-mounted rudder from before the 1st century CE is already called a junk; the battened junk sail was probably Southeast Asian in origin, first shown at the Bayon temple at Angkor Thom.

notes: Dated to the sea-going junk of the Song (the bulkheads attested by 1119), since the earlier river junk's one firm trace, the Han pottery model with a stern rudder, is already the sternpost-rudder node (50 CE). The article says junks relied on the compass (built: magnetic-compass, 1088). Left out a paragraph on Huan Ji and a sea monster in the Yuan section, which reads as vandalism.

entry.name: Dhow
entry.desc: Dhow is the general name for a number of traditional sailing vessels of the Red Sea and Indian Ocean, with one or more masts carrying settee or sometimes lateen sails. Their exact origins are lost, but most scholars believe the dhow arose in India between 600 BCE and 600 CE. Dhows carried heavy cargo along the coasts of Eastern Arabia, Iran, East Africa and South Asia; Omanis and the Hadhrami people of Yemen had theirs built at Beypore in Kerala, their hull planks once held together by coconut rope. They were used extensively in the Red Sea and Indian Ocean slave trades, and some still sail between the Persian Gulf and East Africa.

row.label: Dhow
row.contested: Some claim that the sanbuk, a type of dhow, derives from the Portuguese caravel, though caravels reached the region only in the late 15th century; another account makes the Somalis the first to use the dhow for trade.

notes: DOUBTFUL: the article gives no firm first evidence, only what most scholars believe (India, 600 BCE to 600 CE); year 0 is the middle of that range, as the tree does with other ranges. Skip it if a node needs firm evidence. Not built on lateen-sail (150 CE), which is later than the range's middle. The Somali 'oldest surviving dhow, the Beden' passage is unsourced in tone and kept only as a claim.

entry.name: Dugout canoe
entry.desc: A dugout canoe, or logboat, is a boat made from a hollowed-out tree, and the oldest boat type archaeologists have found. Before metal tools the log was hollowed with controlled fires and the burnt wood removed with an adze. The Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, carbon dated to between 8040 and 7510 BCE, is believed to be the world's oldest boat; the Dufuna canoe of Nigeria and a dugout from Kuahuqiao in Zhejiang, China, are both about 8,000 years old. Dugouts could be fitted with outriggers for rougher water, and they are still paddled and punted on lakes and rivers in Africa and Asia.

row.label: Dugout canoe
row.contested: Dugouts may be the oldest boats found only because their massive wood survives better than lighter craft such as bark canoes.

notes: Year is the middle of the Pesse canoe's carbon date. The 'also' finds are on other continents and of about the same age; the article does not say outright that they were invented independently. Built on fire and stone tools: the article says logs were hollowed by controlled fires and adzes.

entry.name: Horseshoe
entry.desc: A horseshoe is a piece of equipment, usually nailed through the hoof wall, that protects a horse's hoof from wear. Its origin is uncertain, since worn iron was usually reforged: bronze shoes with apparent nail holes come from an Etruscan tomb of around 400 BCE, iron remnants from tombs in northeast China of the Goguryeo period dated to 414 CE, and a shoe with its nails from the tomb of the Frankish king Childeric I at Tournai. Written records of nailed shoes begin around 900 CE; by the Crusades horseshoes were widespread in Europe, and in China iron shoes became common under the Yuan dynasty.

row.label: Horseshoe
row.contested: Four bronze horseshoes with what seem to be nail holes, found in an Etruscan tomb of around 400 BCE, may be older, and Catullus's 'mule shoes' may mean the Roman hipposandal rather than a nailed shoe; there is no hard evidence that the Druids invented it.

notes: Historians differ on the origin. 414 CE (Goguryeo tombs) is the earliest dated find the article states without a hedge; the Etruscan find ('apparently nail holes') goes into contested. civ left empty: the article does not credit Goguryeo with the invention. Childeric's tomb is dated only 'fifth century'.

entry.name: Spear-thrower
entry.desc: A spear-thrower, or atlatl, is a lever, usually about as long as the user's arm or forearm, with a cup or spur that holds the butt of a dart or javelin and throws it faster than the arm alone could. It is believed to have been used by Homo sapiens since the Upper Paleolithic, and the earliest known example is a Solutrean spear-thrower of reindeer antler, 17,500 years old, from Combe Saunière in the Dordogne, France. Ice Age hunters used it against megafauna; in Europe the bow and arrow supplemented it, while it stayed in use in the Americas, where Teotihuacan's warriors carried it, and in Australia as the woomera.

row.label: Spear-thrower
row.contested: It may be older: it is believed to have been in use from around 30,000 years ago, and the arthritic right elbow of Mungo Man, of 42,000 BP, has been read as 'atlatl elbow'.

notes: Entry dates left empty: the only date is five digits (17,500 years ago), which the site's parser would misread; it stays in the desc and the row's date. Year -15500 = 17,500 years before present. The Americas not given as an independent origin: the article says it may have come over the Bering Land Bridge.

entry.name: Bayonet
entry.desc: A bayonet is a knife, dagger, sword or spike mounted on the barrel of a musket or rifle, so that the gun can be used as a spear in close combat. The first recorded bayonet proper is the 'gun-knife' of the son-and-mother gun in the Chinese military treatise Binglu of 1606, a plug bayonet pushed into the barrel. Jean Martinet standardized plug bayonets for new French fusilier regiments in 1671; because they stopped the gun from firing, socket bayonets that fitted around the barrel replaced them, and by the mid-18th century most European armies had adopted these for massed infantry charges.

row.label: Bayonet
row.contested: The word bayonette is older, from the 16th century, but it is unclear whether it then named a knife fitted to a gun; its supposed origin in the town of Bayonne has no basis in fact.

notes: civ left empty: the article says only 'Chinese' and does not name the Ming. The son-and-mother gun is called a breech-loading musket, so built: musket (1521).

entry.name: Torpedo
entry.desc: A torpedo is a self-propelled underwater weapon with an explosive warhead that detonates on contact with or close to its target. The word first named mines and spar torpedoes, used by Cornelius Drebbel, Robert Fulton and in the American Civil War. In 1864 the naval officer Giovanni Luppis gave the English engineer Robert Whitehead plans for a floating weapon at Fiume, now Rijeka in Croatia; Whitehead made from it the first modern self-propelled torpedo, run underwater by compressed air, and presented it to the Austrian Imperial Naval commission on 21 December 1866. On 16 January 1878 the Turkish steamer Intibah became the first ship sunk by self-propelled torpedoes.

row.label: Torpedo
row.contested: Around 1280 Hasan al-Rammah described a rocket-driven incendiary craft that moved across the water, often cited as an early torpedo, but historians class it as a surface-skimming rocket; until about 1900 the word also covered mines and spar torpedoes.

notes: civ Austrian Empire (the profile runs to 1867): the article has the Austrian Imperial Naval commission receive it and the Austrian government invest in its production. It calls Fiume a port of the 'Austro-Hungarian Monarchy', anachronistic for 1866, so the desc avoids the phrase. No parent on the tree fits plainly.

entry.name: Rifling
entry.desc: Rifling is the helical grooving cut inside a gun barrel to spin the projectile, steadying its flight and making it more accurate. Its inventor is not known: straight 'soot grooves' were cut in small arms from at least 1480, and among the earliest recorded spiral-grooved barrels are those of the Vienna gunsmith Gaspard Kollner in 1498 and of Augustus Kotter of Nuremberg in 1520. Because the grooves had to be engraved by hand, rifled guns were at first used mostly by wealthy hunters, and they became common only in the mid-19th century; the first practical military rifled weapons were breech-loaders such as the Queen Anne pistol.

row.label: Rifling
row.contested: Gaspard Kollner of Vienna made spiral-grooved barrels as early as 1498 by some accounts, but some scholars hold that his grooves were straight until Kotter helped him.

notes: 1520 (Kotter) taken as firm, 1498 (Kollner) as disputed, as the article reports. The article speaks of 'musket barrels', but the musket node is dated 1521, a year later, so built: arquebus (1411).

entry.name: Crane
entry.desc: A crane is a machine that lifts and moves loads with a boom, hoist, ropes or chains and sheaves, using levers and pulleys for mechanical advantage. The shaduf, a crane-like lever for lifting irrigation water, was used in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, but building cranes appear in Greece in the late 6th century BCE, attested by cuttings for lifting tongs and Lewis irons on temple blocks. The Romans added pulleys and treadwheels: a polyspastos worked by four men could lift 3,000 kg. Treadwheel cranes returned to Europe in the High Middle Ages for Gothic cathedrals and harbours, and steam engines, then internal combustion engines and electric motors, later powered them.

row.label: Crane
row.contested: The shaduf of ancient Mesopotamia is sometimes counted as the first crane, but it was a lever for lifting irrigation water.

notes: Built on the shaduf, a candidate of another batch of this release (the article calls it 'the first known crane machine'; d-1.json has it at c. 2200 BCE from its own article, so the crane article's 'around 3000 BCE' was left out to avoid a contradiction). Run the checker with d-1.json to resolve the parent. civ empty: the article speaks of Greek city-states generally, and there is no Ancient Greece profile. Left out the 'Persian Innovations' paragraph (it calls al-Jazari of the Artuqid court Persian).
